blocks.text: Treating viral infections is fundamentally different from bacterial treatment. Bacteria are independent organisms, while viruses are parasites. Unlike bacteria, which are living organisms on their own, viruses are not truly alive. Viruses live inside our cells and use our own DNA/RNA machinery to replicate. This makes it hard to develop a drug that kills the virus without harming our healthy human cells.

Viruses can change their genetic material very quickly. This is called mutation. A drug that works against a virus one year might not work the next because the virus has changed. This is why flu vaccines need to be updated every year.
highlight: Viruses can change their genetic material very quickly. This is called mutation.

blocks.text: Viruses also integrate into our genome and stay asleep for years. Drugs at recent times can kill only active viruses and not those which have been sleeping for years.

Antiviral medications work by targeting specific stages of the viral life cycle. For example, some antivirals prevent the virus from entering our cells, while others stop the virus from making copies of its genetic material. One of the most common mechanisms of action of antiviral drugs is enzyme inhibition. For example, protease inhibitor, does not allow the virus to produce their protein in one long strand. These inhibitors also help in the treatment of HIV and hepatitis C infections. Some antiviral drugs enhance the immune response to viral infections. Interferons are proteins that can boost immune system to fight against viruses.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The virus does make its proteins as one long strand (a polyprotein). A protease inhibitor stops the viral protease cutting this strand into working proteins.

blocks.prompt: a) Drug A has a TI of 3, and Drug B has a TI of 50. Which drug is considered safer, and why?
blocks.explanation: Drug B. Its toxic dose is 50 times its effective dose, whereas for Drug A it is only 3 times, so B has a much larger safety margin.

blocks.prompt: b) How do antacids (e.g., magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂) chemically regulate stomach pH? Write a simple neutralization equation to illustrate this.
blocks.explanation: An antacid is a base; it neutralises excess HCl in the stomach and raises the pH: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.

blocks.prompt: c) Identify the core, strained heterocyclic ring system in penicillin that is essential for its antibacterial activity.
blocks.explanation: The four-membered beta-lactam ring (fused to a thiazolidine ring).

blocks.prompt: d) Compare the chemical structures of morphine and codeine (methylmorphine). How does this small structural difference relate to codeine's action as a prodrug?
blocks.explanation: Codeine is morphine in which one phenolic OH group is changed to OCH₃. Because of this, codeine binds weakly to opioid receptors; in the liver its methyl group is removed and it becomes morphine, which provides most of the pain relief. Codeine is therefore a prodrug (a drug converted into the active drug inside the body).

rows: –OCH₃ group in the same position (the H of –OH replaced by methyl)
A prodrug: in the liver the –CH₃ is removed to give morphine, which gives most of the pain relief

blocks.prompt: e) Why do many antiviral drugs cause significant side effects for the host patient?
blocks.explanation: A virus copies itself using the machinery of the host's own cells, so a drug that stops the virus can also interfere with the work of the patient's healthy cells.
